a: The problem of free will is one of the most enduring debates in philosophy. It concerns whether humans have the ability to make genuinely free choices or whether all actions are determined by prior causes. Hard determinism holds that determinism is true and free will is an illusion. According to this view, every event, including human action, is causally determined by preceding events and natural laws, leaving no room for genuine choice. Libertarian free will argues that humans do have free will, and that determinism is false. This position requires that some events, particularly human decisions, are not fully determined by prior causes. Compatibilism attempts to reconcile free will with determinism by redefining free will. Compatibilists argue that as long as a person acts according to their own desires and intentions without external coercion, their actions are free, even if those desires themselves are causally determined. Modern neuroscience has added new dimensions to the debate, with experiments suggesting that brain activity associated with decisions occurs before conscious awareness of the decision. However, the philosophical implications of these findings continue to be debated.

The philosophy of consciousness addresses fundamental questions about the nature of subjective experience. The hard problem of consciousness, articulated by David Chalmers, asks why and how physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective, qualitative experiences (qualia). This is distinguished from easy problems of consciousness, which involve explaining cognitive functions like attention, memory, and behavior. Dualism, most famously associated with René Descartes, holds that mind and matter are fundamentally different substances. The mind is non-physical and interacts with the physical body. Materialism or physicalism holds that consciousness is entirely a product of physical processes in the brain, and all mental phenomena can be explained in neural terms. Functionalism argues that mental states are defined by their causal relationships rather than their physical substrate, meaning consciousness could theoretically exist in non-biological systems. Panpsychism suggests that consciousness is a fundamental feature of all matter, with even elementary particles possessing some form of proto-consciousness. Integrated information theory, proposed by Giulio Tononi, attempts to measure consciousness mathematically. Despite centuries of inquiry, the nature of consciousness remains one of philosophy's deepest mysteries.

Existentialism is a philosophical movement that emphasizes individual existence, freedom, and choice. It emerged in the 19th and 20th centuries, with key figures including Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, and Albert Camus. The central premise of existentialism is that existence precedes essence, meaning that humans are not born with a predetermined purpose but must create their own meaning through choices and actions. Kierkegaard emphasized the importance of personal commitment and the leap of faith in religion. Nietzsche declared that God is dead and humans must create their own values in a world without inherent meaning. Sartre argued that humans are condemned to be free, forced to make choices and take responsibility for their actions. Camus developed the philosophy of the absurd, arguing that humans seek meaning in a meaningless universe, and proposed embracing the absurd condition without resignation. Existentialism has had profound influence on literature, psychology, and political thought.

Stoicism is an ancient Greek and Roman philosophy founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE. It teaches the development of self-control and fortitude as a means to overcome destructive emotions. The core Stoic belief is that virtue (wisdom, justice, courage, and moderation) is the highest good and that external circumstances, such as wealth, health, and reputation, are indifferent to true happiness. The Stoics divide things into what is up to us (our thoughts, judgments, and actions) and what is not up to us (everything else, including the actions of others, our health, and our reputation). Happiness comes from focusing only on what we can control. Key Stoic practices include negative visualization (imagining losing what we value to appreciate it more), the view from above (seeing our problems in the context of the cosmos), and voluntary discomfort (temporarily embracing hardship to build resilience). Prominent Stoic philosophers include Epictetus, a former slave whose Discourses teach practical wisdom; Seneca, a Roman statesman who wrote extensively on ethics; and Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor whose Meditations provide personal reflections on Stoic practice. Modern Stoicism has experienced a revival as a practical philosophy for resilience and well-being.

The trolley problem is a famous ethical thought experiment introduced by philosopher Philippa Foot in 1967 and later developed by Judith Jarvis Thomson. It presents a moral dilemma: a runaway trolley is heading toward five people tied to the tracks. You can pull a lever to divert the trolley onto a side track, where it will kill one person instead. The question is whether it is morally permissible to pull the lever. This dilemma highlights the conflict between utilitarianism (choosing the action that produces the greatest good for the greatest number, which would favor pulling the lever) and deontological ethics (which might prohibit actively causing harm to an innocent person). Variations of the problem include the fat man variant, where you must push a large man off a footbridge to stop the trolley, creating a more direct conflict between action and inaction. Most people find pushing the fat man much more objectionable than pulling the lever, even though both result in one death versus five. The trolley problem reveals important distinctions in moral reasoning, including the distinction between doing and allowing harm, and between intended and foreseen consequences.
